603.title: the leap decided
603.hook: the strongest one on the beach is the only one who hasn't said a word, and an old bear walks over to remind him who he is
603.howItsDone: Jambavan reminding Hanuman of his strength is one of the best-known scenes in Hindu storytelling, and in many homes and temples it is told before the recitation of the Sundara Kanda begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday: yojana. Ten, twenty, thirty, ninety, and no one could promise a hundred.

Some people never put their hand up. Not because they can't do the thing, but because it hasn't occurred to them that they could. On the beach, while the others called out their numbers, Hanuman sat to one side, silent. Valmiki doesn't give him a line in the whole count. So Jambavan, the oldest one there, the one who knows everybody's story, gets up, walks over, and sits down beside him.
screen: `HANUMAN SITS APART.` → `NOT ONE WORD IN THE COUNT.` → `JAMBAVAN WALKS OVER.`

segments.voice: Jambavan tells Hanuman his own story. Your mother was Anjana. Your father is Vayu, the wind. As a baby you saw the sun coming up, thought it was a ripe fruit, and jumped for it, straight into the sky. Indra, king of the gods, threw his thunderbolt, you fell, and your jaw was struck. In Sanskrit the jaw is hanu, and that's where your name comes from. The wind god was so grieved he stopped blowing, and the gods gave you gifts to set things right. Then Jambavan says what he came to say: you have your father's speed. Why are you sitting there? Hanuman stands up. Valmiki describes him growing, filling with strength, roaring until the others cheer. He'll leap the ocean, he says, find Sita, and come back. He climbs Mount Mahendra by the shore to push off from, and there the Kishkindha Kanda, the book of the monkey kingdom, ends: on a mountaintop, before the jump. Why did he need reminding at all? Valmiki's scene doesn't fully say. A curse in the Uttara Kanda, the last book, which many scholars think was added later, says sages once made him forget his strength until someone recalled it. Many families tell it that way. Either way, sometimes strength comes back when someone else remembers it out loud.

604.title: the leap
604.hook: the Sundara Kanda opens with a monkey pressing his feet into a mountain so hard that water runs out of the rock
604.carry: an arrow loosed from Rama's bow
604.howItsDone: Many Hindus recite the Sundara Kanda in full at home or in temples, often over several days, and some families read it in times of difficulty or before a new undertaking.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hanu. Jambavan told Hanuman his own story, and Hanuman stood up and climbed Mount Mahendra.

Of the seven books of the Ramayana, this is the one many Hindu families read on its own, start to finish, sometimes over days, sometimes when life is hard. It's the Sundara Kanda, the beautiful book. And it begins mid-breath. The first verse opens, tato rāvaṇanītāyāḥ sītāyāḥ śatrukarśanaḥ: then, the tamer of enemies, of Sita, carried off by Ravana. It goes on: he set out to find her trail, along the path the sky-travelers use. No warm-up. Just: then.
screen: `THE BOOK MANY FAMILIES READ WHOLE.` → `SUNDARA: THE BEAUTIFUL BOOK.` → `IT BEGINS WITH 'THEN.'`

segments.voice: Hanuman stands on Mahendra, and Valmiki slows everything down. Hanuman presses his hands and feet into the mountain. The rock gives. Streams burst out of it. Colored minerals run down its sides like paint. Animals bolt from their caves, snakes come out hissing, and sages and celestial beings rise into the air to get out of the way. A whole mountain shakes because one being is gathering himself. Then Hanuman says what he'll do. He'll go to Lanka like an arrow loosed from Rama's bow. If Sita isn't there, he'll search heaven. If he can't find her, he'll pull up Lanka and bring Ravana back bound. A big speech, and Valmiki lets him make it. Then he crouches, tucks his ears back, draws in his breath, and springs. Notice the comparison he chooses. Not a bird, not the wind, though he's the wind's son. An arrow from Rama's bow: he isn't going for himself; he's the shot Rama is firing across the sea. Why is the book called beautiful? Valmiki never says. People give different answers: that Hanuman himself was called Sundara, that it's where hope returns, that its pictures of Lanka are the loveliest in the epic. All of those are told, and none is Valmiki's. What the text gives us is its first word: then. The story was stuck on a beach. Now it moves.

605.title: the leap
605.hook: when Hanuman takes off, the trees on the mountain are pulled along behind him, and fall one by one into the sea
605.carry: trees falling like family at the gate
605.howItsDone: Devotional paintings often show Hanuman in midair over the sea, sometimes with flowers falling around him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman pressed the mountain until water ran from the rock, and sprang like an arrow loosed from Rama's bow.

Valmiki gives Hanuman's leap an escort. The force of his takeoff tears the flowering trees on Mahendra loose, and they fly up after him. It's a picture from ordinary life, borrowed for a mountain: the parent at the school gate, the one who comes as far as they can and then has to stop. Hanuman is about to cross a hundred yojanas alone, and the trees go with him as far as trees can.
screen: `THE TREES FLY AFTER HIM.` → `AS FAR AS THEY CAN GO.`

segments.voice: Valmiki makes the comparison himself: the trees follow Hanuman for a while like relatives seeing off someone dear, and then, one by one, they drop into the ocean, and their blossoms float on the dark water like stars in the sky. A hero is crossing the sea to find a stolen queen, and Valmiki stops to watch petals on the water. Some readers say this is part of why the book is called beautiful. Then he turns to Hanuman. His outstretched arms look like great serpents rising from a mountain. His eyes shine like fire. His tail curves up behind him. His shadow on the sea moves across the waves like a ship under sail. The wind roars, the water churns where he passes, and the gods, the celestial singers and the great sages watch from the sky and shower him with flowers and praise. The whole world is part of this one crossing: the trees below, the sea, the sky above. And yet Hanuman is alone. Nobody can go with him. The trees tried, and fell. Whatever waits on the other side, he meets by himself. But he leaves carrying the trees' farewell, the sea's attention and the sky's good wishes. Alone isn't the same as unaccompanied.

606.title: Mainaka
606.hook: halfway across the sea, a golden mountain rises out of the water and offers Hanuman a place to rest
606.carry: your welcome is as good as done
606.howItsDone: In Sundara Kanda recitations, Mainaka is remembered as the first of three meetings over the sea, and Hanuman's touch of the mountain is often explained as accepting the hospitality without stopping.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the long flight, trees falling like family at the gate, and a shadow sailing on the sea.

You're driving a long way, late, and a friend texts: you're passing my town, come in, I've made dinner, sleep here. It's a real kindness. But if you stop, you won't get where you're going in time. That's the first test Hanuman meets over the ocean, and it isn't a monster. It's a gift. The sea has been watching him, and the sea feels it owes him something.
screen: `COME IN, I'VE MADE DINNER.` → `THE FIRST TEST IS A GIFT.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki's telling, the Ocean is a person who thinks and remembers, and it remembers a debt. Long ago King Sagara, an ancestor of Rama's own line, had sons who dug out the bed of the sea; tradition says that's why the ocean is called sagara. So the Ocean thinks: this monkey is on an errand for Rama, of the family that made me what I am. He shouldn't wear himself out. It calls to a mountain hidden beneath its waves, Mainaka, to rise and give the traveler a place to rest. Mainaka lifts out of the water, golden peaks shining, trees on his slopes, takes a human form on the summit, and invites Hanuman to rest, eat fruit, and then go on. Hanuman's first reaction is suspicion: a mountain rising in his path looks like an obstacle, and he pushes it aside with his chest. Then Mainaka explains, and Hanuman understands. He answers with great courtesy. I'm grateful. Your welcome is as good as done. But time is pressing, and I've promised not to stop on the way. He touches the mountain with his hand, honoring the offer, and flies on. Refusing a threat is easy to understand. Refusing kindness without hurting the one who offers it takes skill. Hanuman doesn't lecture, and he doesn't rest a little to be polite. He receives the gift by touching it, and keeps his promise.

607.title: Mainaka
607.hook: once, the story goes, mountains had wings, and one of them owes its wings to Hanuman's father
607.carry: a breath of wind long ago
607.howItsDone: The story of the winged mountains and Indra's thunderbolt is told in several Hindu texts, and in Sundara Kanda recitations Mainaka's speech is often read as a picture of gratitude carried across generations.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mainaka rose from the sea to offer rest, and Hanuman said no, thank you, with a hand on the summit.

Sometimes a stranger is kind to you, and later you find out why. Your grandmother taught their mother to read. Your dad once pulled their car out of a ditch in the snow. The kindness was a thank-you that had waited years for someone from your family to come along. When Mainaka rises from the sea, the Ocean has one reason to help. Mainaka, it turns out, has his own.
screen: `A STRANGER'S KINDNESS, EXPLAINED.` → `A THANK-YOU THAT WAITED YEARS.`

segments.voice: Mainaka tells Hanuman a story from the earliest age of the world. In those days, he says, the mountains had wings. They flew wherever they pleased, fast as the wind, and the sages and creatures below lived in fear one would come down on them. So Indra, king of the gods, took up his thunderbolt and went after the mountains, cutting off their wings one after another. When Indra came for Mainaka, the wind god Vayu swept him out of reach and dropped him safely into the ocean, wings and all. Vayu, Mainaka reminds Hanuman, is your father. So I owe you. Helping you is how I pay your father back. Hold that next to yesterday. The Ocean helps because of Rama's ancestors; Mainaka helps because of Hanuman's father. Two old debts from two families, coming due on the same crossing. In Valmiki's world, kindness doesn't disappear. It sinks below the surface, sometimes for ages, and rises when the right person passes. And there's a last turn. Indra, the very god who cut the mountains' wings, is pleased at what Mainaka has done for Rama's messenger, and grants him safety. An old enmity is set aside for one good deed done for someone else's cause. Here the idea of karma, that actions bear fruit, is told not as a law but as a scene. A breath of wind long ago means a resting place today.
screen: `MOUNTAINS ONCE HAD WINGS.` · `INDRA CUTS THEM; VAYU SAVES MAINAKA.` · `TWO OLD DEBTS COME DUE.` · then, large: `INDRA GRANTS MAINAKA SAFETY.`

segments.voice: Think of a kindness someone in your family did long ago, one you've only heard about, and hold that story. Then think of a kindness you could do that might not be repaid for years, or ever. Let both rest together as you breathe, the old one and the possible one.

A coach who keeps raising the bar every time you clear it. Some tests aren't trying to stop you; they're trying to see what you do when force won't work. Over the open sea, Mainaka behind him, Hanuman flies straight into one of those. And the ones who set it up aren't his enemies. They're the gods, who want to know what this monkey is really made of.
screen: `THE BAR KEEPS RISING.` → `THE GODS SET THE TEST.`

segments.voice: The gods, the celestial musicians and the great sages talk it over. They ask Surasa, the mother of the nagas, the serpent beings, to take a terrifying form and block Hanuman's way, so they can see his strength and his cleverness. Surasa rises from the sea huge and frightening: the gods have given you to me as food, she says. You have to enter my mouth. Hanuman doesn't attack. He talks. Briefly and honestly he tells her who he is and why he's here: Rama, the forest, Sita taken, the search. He asks her to let him pass. Then he makes a remarkable offer. Let me find Sita and tell Rama, and I promise I'll come back and enter your mouth. The errand comes first; his own life can wait in line behind it. Surasa refuses. She has a boon, she says, that no one can get past her. And she opens her mouth. So Hanuman grows to ten yojanas, too big to swallow. She opens wider, twenty. He grows to thirty; she opens to forty. On they go, each matching the other, until her mouth gapes a hundred yojanas wide, as wide as the sea he's crossing. Every time he gets bigger, she gets bigger. Force won't settle this. Hanuman, hovering there, has to think of something else.

609.title: Surasa
609.hook: with her mouth a hundred yojanas wide, Hanuman wins by becoming the size of a thumb
609.howItsDone: Many Hindu tellers, from grandparents to temple storytellers, use Surasa's test to show that Hanuman's wisdom matters as much as his strength, and devotional art often shows the tiny Hanuman beside her vast mouth.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Surasa, mother of serpents, and a mouth that grew every time Hanuman did.

Out over the open sea, a monkey grown to the size of a mountain hangs in the air. In front of him, a serpent mother's jaws gape a hundred yojanas wide. Every time he has grown, Surasa's mouth has grown wider, and the gods are watching. He's been answering size with size. Now, Valmiki says, in the blink of an eye, he does the opposite.
screen: `A MOUTH A HUNDRED YOJANAS WIDE.` → `SIZE AGAINST SIZE.` → `IN A BLINK, THE OPPOSITE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman makes himself tiny, about the size of a thumb. He darts into Surasa's enormous mouth and, before she can close it, darts back out. Then he stops in the air, bows, and speaks respectfully. I've entered your mouth, so your boon is kept. Now I'm going on to find Sita. He hasn't broken her rule; he's honored it, completely and literally. He hasn't broken his promise to Rama either. Both are kept at once. No fight, no wound, no loser. Surasa is delighted. She sets aside the frightening form, appears as herself, and blesses him: go, find Sita, bring her and Rama together. The gods who set the test cheer. They wanted to see his strength and his cleverness, and they saw both: strength enough to grow vast, and cleverness enough to know when growing is the wrong answer. That closes a week of crossings. It began with Jambavan sitting beside a silent Hanuman and telling him his own story. Then Mahendra shaking, water from the rock, the arrow from Rama's bow. Trees falling into the sea like relatives turning back at the gate. Mainaka rising with the Ocean's thanks and his own, and Hanuman's polite touch. And now Surasa, met not with a bigger force but a smaller, wiser one. Three tests so far: courage, courtesy, cleverness. One more meeting waits over the sea, and it is not a test.
screen: `HANUMAN BECOMES THUMB-SIZED.` · `IN AND OUT; HER BOON IS KEPT.` · `SURASA BLESSES HIM.` · then, large: `A WEEK OF CROSSINGS.`

segments.voice: Let your breathing become small and quiet, the way Hanuman becomes small: shoulders soft, hands loose, no need to take up extra room. If a thought pushes in, don't push back; let it pass through, the way Hanuman passes in and out. Small, quiet, awake.
